title: Alaska Packers’ Association v. Domenico
summary: The fishermen’s promise to perform the same work they already owed did not support a midseason promise to double their fixed compensation.
notes:
The notes reproduce New York General Obligations Law § 5-1103 and contrast UCC § 2-209. Those are separate routes for assessing modifications. The case does not establish that every later increase in compensation fails.

117 F. 99 (9th Cir. 1902). The March 1900 contracts paid $50 for the season; a second group signed in April at $60 for the season plus two cents per salmon, and both groups joined the demand for $100 after arriving at Pyramid Harbor.

sections.Parties: The fishermen sought additional seasonal wages from Alaska Packers. The company appealed the admiralty judgment entered for the fishermen.
sections.Material Facts:
The workers signed contracts in San Francisco to sail to Pyramid Harbor, Alaska, and perform shipboard, fishing, loading, and other assigned work. Each was to receive $50 for the season plus two cents for each red salmon in whose catching he participated. After reaching the remote cannery, the workers stopped together and demanded $100 for their services, threatening to stop entirely and return to San Francisco. Alaska Packers had substantial capital invested in the cannery, the fishing season was short, and substitute labor was unavailable. Its superintendent signed the higher-pay agreement under that pressure. The workers completed the season, but the company paid according to the original contracts.

The workers argued that defective fishing nets justified their demand. The evidence on the nets conflicted, and the trial judge found against them. The appellate court accepted that finding. The superintendent had also told the workers that he lacked authority to alter their contracts; the appellate court assumed authority for purposes of addressing consideration.
sections.Procedural History: The fishermen sued in admiralty and won the additional compensation. The Ninth Circuit reversed. It treated the findings about the nets as settled and decided the consideration issue as a question of law; its reasoning did not require a final determination that the superintendent possessed authority.
sections.Issue: Did the promise to continue the exact services already required by the original agreements provide consideration for the promise of higher wages?
sections.Holding: No. On the findings accepted by the court, the employees promised no new performance, and the higher-wage promise was unenforceable for want of consideration.
sections.Reasoning:
The original contracts already required the services demanded. Continuing that work therefore added no bargained-for legal detriment or new entitlement for the company. The timing of the stoppage mattered because the workers used the company’s inability to replace them to extract additional pay. The court refused to characterize the transaction as a voluntary abandonment of the original agreement followed by an independent new bargain. Nor could the workers make the promise enforceable merely by performing the work afterward: that performance was already owed, and reliance generated by their own wrongful pressure did not supply the missing consideration.

This decision illustrates the pre-existing-duty approach to modifications. Its source of invalidity is the absence of new consideration, reinforced by the circumstances of coercion. Later assigned materials examine other approaches to modification and the separate defense of economic duress; those approaches must be evaluated under their own requirements.

textbookImport.basis: Study paraphrase of the supplied tenth-edition casebook. No current-law/citator review.

learning.why: It connects consideration to contract modification and shows why a promise to pay more for unchanged performance can raise both an exchange problem and a coercion problem.

topics.consideration: Performance already owed to the same promisor supplied no new consideration.
topics.modification: The court rejected the midseason wage increase.
topics.duress: Remote location, short season, and unavailable replacements explain the pressure; the judgment rests on consideration.
topics.assent: The court declined to treat the pressured wage change as a voluntary rescission and new agreement.
topics.legal-detriment: The pre-existing duty rule is a legal-detriment problem: promising what one is already bound to do surrenders no freedom and so cannot be consideration.
topics.good-faith-early: The fishermen's coercive midseason demand is the classic bad-faith modification that later UCC 2-209 comment 2 and Restatement 89 are designed to police.

mnemonic.rationale: Fishermen who wanted a raise at sea
